reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: A group of monogenic, autosomal dominant forms of diabetes caused by single-gene defects impairing beta-cell function rather than autoimmunity or insulin resistance
Suspect it in young, non-obese patients with diabetes across several generations and a strong family history consistent with dominant inheritance
Patients are typically negative for islet autoantibodies and retain measurable endogenous insulin (detectable C-peptide) beyond the honeymoon period
It is frequently misclassified as type 1 or type 2 diabetes, so a high index of suspicion and genetic testing are key to correct diagnosis
The specific gene determines the phenotype and treatment: some forms are mild and stable, others progressive
One common subtype often causes mild, stable, non-progressive fasting hyperglycaemia that may need no pharmacological treatment
Another common subtype is characteristically sensitive to sulfonylureas, so accurate genetic diagnosis can allow a change away from insulin
Correct diagnosis has implications for prognosis, treatment choice, family screening, and, in some subtypes, pregnancy management
reference.pathophysiology: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young comprises several monogenic disorders in which a mutation in a single gene critical to pancreatic beta-cell development or function impairs insulin secretion. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so an affected parent transmits the condition to roughly half of offspring, producing diabetes across successive generations at a young age. Unlike type 1 diabetes, there is no autoimmune beta-cell destruction, and unlike type 2 diabetes, obesity and insulin resistance are not central. Different causative genes give distinct clinical pictures, ranging from mild stable hyperglycaemia due to an altered glucose-sensing threshold, to progressive insulin secretory failure with risk of the usual diabetes complications.
additionalDifferentials: Type 2 diabetes mellitus in the young
Neonatal diabetes and other monogenic beta-cell disorders
Gestational diabetes when first detected in pregnancy
additionalInvestigations: Islet autoantibody panel to help exclude autoimmune diabetes
C-peptide to demonstrate preserved endogenous insulin secretion
Detailed multigenerational family history of diabetes
Genetic testing of the relevant MODY genes to confirm the subtype
Assessment for extra-pancreatic features associated with certain subtypes such as renal cysts
Cascade genetic screening of at-risk family members
redFlags: Presentation with ketoacidosis, which is atypical and suggests type 1 diabetes instead
Rapidly progressive hyperglycaemia inconsistent with a mild stable subtype
Associated renal or genitourinary abnormalities suggesting a specific syndromic subtype
Diagnostic uncertainty leading to inappropriate lifelong insulin in a sulfonylurea-responsive form
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies by subtype: the mild glucose-sensing form is typically stable with low complication risk and may need no treatment, whereas transcription-factor subtypes are progressive and can develop classic microvascular and macrovascular complications if hyperglycaemia is uncontrolled; accurate genetic diagnosis enables tailored, often simpler, management.
pitfalls: Automatically labelling young-onset diabetes as type 1 and committing to lifelong insulin without considering monogenic causes
Overlooking the family history that suggests dominant inheritance
Failing to check autoantibodies and C-peptide before classification
Not offering genetic testing that could change treatment and enable family screening
